definition: Cajole means to persuade with flattery and gentle coaxing.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word cajole. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know cajole should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: It took the twins twenty minutes of compliments and cocoa to cajole their grandfather into one more chapter of the bedtime book.
A nudge merely floats the idea and hopes; it stops far short of cajole's smiling campaign of compliments.
Coax goes further than a nudge — you are actively, gently persuading — but cajole outdoes coax by layering flattery over sheer cheerful persistence.

To wheedle is cajole's needier cousin: the coaxing turns whiny and self-serving, wearing a person down with pleading. Cajoling stays sunnier, all flattery and good humor, with the target still smiling as the yes arrives.
To flatter is to serve up praise and stop there — the compliment is the whole act. To cajole puts the praise to work, aiming compliments, warmth, and cheerful patience at winning a yes.

To entice is to tempt someone by dangling something they want — the reward does the persuading. To cajole works through the persuader's own charm instead: compliments, teasing, and patient good humor carry the person to yes.
to bully someone into agreement with scowls and pressure
to force a result through raw power, no charm involved

Cajole arrived intact from French cajoler. One theory hears a bird chattering sweetly in its cage; another points to an old word for chattering like a jay. The trail is disputed, and no piece of it survives anywhere else in English, so the word stands alone.
Cajole means to persuade with flattery and gentle coaxing.

Nobody could get the retired violinist to play at the street fair until the baker set about cajoling her: praise for her old recordings, a joke about the trombonist needing rescue, a warm loaf sent over each morning for a week.
By Saturday she was tuning up on the bakery steps, still insisting she had agreed to nothing.
Cajole names one specific route to yes: flattery and gentle, good-humored coaxing, applied patiently.
Pressure, threats and blunt argument are persuasion too, but they are not cajolery — the cajoler keeps you smiling while you give in.
Cajole is the word for winning someone over with charm — flattery, teasing, patience — never force.
Coax covers any gentle persuading; wheedle is cajole's needier cousin.
The moment pressure or threats enter, you have left cajoling for browbeating.

The documentary crew had one week to cajole the island's last lighthouse keeper into an interview he had refused for thirty years.
They did not offer money, and they knew better than to beg.
Instead they praised his garden, laughed at his jokes, carried his firewood, and asked again each evening with the same good humor.

On the sixth day he set two chairs by the lamp room and said, 'One hour, and you'll take some tomatoes home.' The director swears the film was won not by the questions but by the week of cheerful patience that came before them.
